title: Reading the classics
hookLine: read the best books first, or you may not get to them (Walden 3)

cards: A stack by the bed. A great book someone meant to finish, the bookmark stalled near the start. On top of it, the phone, which is easier to pick up.
Thoreau lived in a one-room cabin with very little furniture, and yet the third chapter of Walden isn't about saws or beans. It's called Reading.
And in his earlier river book, he left advice that sounds simple and stings a little: read the best books first, or you may never get to them at all.

teach.b: First, the order of things. The best books first is a line about time. Life is short, and reading hours are few.
Fill them with whatever's nearest, and the great things wait forever. It's yesterday's simplify, applied to a bookshelf.
Second, how to read: "Books must be read as deliberately and reservedly as they were written." Slowly, with attention, one considered sentence at a time.
He compares real reading to a kind of exercise, something that asks you to stand on tiptoe, not something to doze over. Third, the book on the table.
Thoreau tells us he kept Homer's Iliad on his table through the summer at the pond, and looked at it only now and then, because there was a house to finish and beans to hoe.
The great book sat there, and he didn't read it as much as he meant to. That honesty is part of the lesson. Even Thoreau had a stack.

teach.h: A NEW ERA FROM A BOOK.
teach.b: Fourth, what a book can do: "How many a man has dated a new era in his life from the reading of a book."
A whole new era, starting from a page. Not every book does that, but you can't know which one will unless you open it.
That's the reason for the best books first: not to be impressive, but so the book that might change your life gets its chance.

how: Some readers of Walden keep one demanding book close at hand and read a little of it slowly each day, in the spirit of Thoreau's chapter on reading.

practice: If a book you consider great is within reach, open it anywhere and read one page, slowly, as deliberately as it was written; if not, bring to mind a sentence from any book that once mattered to you.
Let one line stay, and turn it over. Notice a single word in it you'd hurried past before; you're not studying, just keeping company with it.
